1:
The chapter opens on an old man settling the one thing he has not yet settled. The witnesses agree on the arithmetic that makes the urgency plain: Abraham was a hundred when Isaac was born and Isaac was forty when he married, so Abraham stands here at about a hundred and forty. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, adds the horizon on either side — Isaac was thirty-seven when Sarah died, and Abraham, living to a hundred and seventy-five, would survive this marriage by thirty-five years and see Esau and Jacob nearly grown. John Calvin, reformed, reads the notice of age as the reason for the errand rather than a detail beside it: old age itself admonished Abraham to order his household while he could, so that when he died peace might be kept among his posterity and the fear of the Lord flourish. His old age, Calvin grants, was still green; but a man who reckons up his years knows when to act.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, sets out the two considerations that moved him — that he was likely to leave the world soon and would be glad to see his son settled first, and that he had an estate to leave, the LORD having blessed him in all things. Henry's chief interest is in the two negatives that govern everything after. Isaac must not marry a daughter of Canaan, because Abraham saw that people degenerating into great wickedness and knew by revelation that they were appointed to ruin, so that such a marriage would be a snare to his son's soul or at least a blot on his name. And Isaac must not go to fetch a wife himself, lest he be tempted to settle where his kindred were. John Wesley says the same in almost the same words, and Henry generalises it: parents disposing of their children should consult the welfare of their souls and their furtherance in the way to heaven.

Calvin puts the prohibition on a footing more theological than prudential. Some suppose Abraham was simply repelled by Canaanite morals; the real reason, Calvin argues, was that God had separated him from them by covenant, and since he was to inherit the land on their overthrow he was commanded to treat them as perpetual enemies. He had lived quietly among them for years, but could not have children in common with them without confounding what God had ordered to be kept distinct. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, adds the older ground, that Canaan already lay under the curse pronounced at Genesis 9:25, and that it would have been inconsistent with prudence and with God's design to join the heir of the promise to one under it.

Where the servant is to go is described as Abraham's country and kindred, and the reformed John Gill is careful that this does not mean Canaan, which was Abraham's by promise but not by possession — it means Mesopotamia, where he was born. Clarke identifies it as the region where his brother Haran's family had settled and where Abraham himself had lived long with Terah, adding that in that family and in Nahor's the true religion had in some sort been preserved, though later much corrupted. Calvin thinks the choice of place was itself persuasive: a woman would come more willingly knowing she was to marry into her own race. He also anticipates the objection that the servant in fact reaches Padan-aram, and answers that Mesopotamia in ordinary usage took in part of Chaldea too, Moses writing not scientifically but in a popular style. Clarke notes that the whole arrangement — parents employing others to seek wives for their sons, and men settled abroad marrying their children at home — is no peculiarity of Abraham's but a custom he had seen still holding in the East.
5:
The servant will not swear before he knows what he is swearing to, and every witness here counts that to his credit. The reformed John Gill calls it prudently done — he was cautious of an oath and wanted to know how far it would bind him. John Calvin, reformed, admires the religious scrupulosity of a man who does not take an oath rashly: what belonged to his own diligence he might lawfully promise under oath, but the outcome depended on another's will, so he properly inserted the exception. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, explains why the exception mattered so much by pointing, with Calmet, to how the ancients understood swearing — they held themselves bound precisely by what was spoken, with no liberty to interpret the intention behind it (compare the case at Joshua 9:18). Calvin notices what the servant does not raise: he asks nothing about Isaac, being so persuaded of his integrity as not to doubt he would acquiesce in his father's will.

Abraham's answer is not a concession but a hardening. Beware thou that thou bring not my son thither again. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, state the ground plainly: Jehovah had taken him from his father's house and promised him this land for a possession. Ellicott, also grammatical-historical, weighs the two principles the betrothal is told so exactly in order to establish, and finds this the weightier of them. Abraham's posterity must not be merged among the Canaanites — but intermarriage within the race was a means to that end, not a binding law for its own sake. Under no circumstances, however, might they go back to Mesopotamia. The race might stay distinct even with a wife of Palestine, though at religious risk; but returning to Padan-aram they were certain to be absorbed, and could look for no higher lot than Laban's descendants attained. Calvin puts the same choice in terms of what Abraham preferred: to live by hope as a stranger in Canaan rather than settle at ease among his relatives in his native soil.

Then the confidence. The LORD God of heaven, who took me from my father's house and swore to give this land to my seed, he shall send his angel before thee. Calvin traces the inference: Abraham argues from two past acts of God — the calling out and the promise of the land — to a third yet to come, and reasons that God, who had helped him throughout his pilgrimage, would guide this journey too, since it was undertaken at his command. Clarke reads the same confidence as a rule about instruments: when earthly ones fail, heavenly ones are employed, and he takes the angel to be probably the Angel of the Covenant. Henry, puritan-evangelical, and Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, both fasten on the ministry itself — God's angels are ministering spirits sent forth not only for the protection but for the guidance of the heirs of promise (Hebrews 1:14). Abraham then grants the exception: if the woman will not follow, thou shalt be clear from this my oath — only bring not my son thither again. Henry draws the caution out of it, that oaths should be taken warily and their matter rightly understood and limited beforehand, since it is a snare to devour that which is holy and afterwards make the enquiry that should have come first.
9:
With his question answered and the limits of the promise fixed, the servant swears — putting his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master. The reformed John Gill notes that he took the oath readily once he was satisfied of its nature and extent. The gesture itself is the chapter's first real dispute. Gill reports the Targum's paraphrase, that the swearing was by the name of the Word of the Lord God. Ellicott, noting that Jacob later required the same of Joseph (Genesis 47:29), argues from the use of "thigh" for the source of posterity (Genesis 46:26; Exodus 1:5) that it was a euphemism for the circumcised member, so that the oath was really by the covenant of which circumcision was the sign. Clarke reaches the same conclusion through the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem, and reads the whole form together: the rite invoking the sign of the covenant, and the words naming God as self-existent, as Lord of heaven, and as the providence of earth. Calvin lays out both the Jewish opinion — a token of a servant's subjection, still practised, he is told, in parts of the East — and the Christian one, that the hand was placed there in honour of the blessed seed; he thinks the former the simpler, and declines to decide. What he insists on is that the rite was not profane, since the name of God is interposed: the servant's hand lay under Abraham's thigh, but he was adjured by the Creator of heaven and earth, who alone may be invoked as witness and judge.

Clarke is the only one to spell out what the oath was understood to mean, and he paraphrases it: as God is unchangeable in his nature and purposes, so shall I be in this engagement — under penalty of forfeiting all expectation of temporal prosperity, the benefits of the covenant, and future glory. He anticipates a modern reader's discomfort with the rite and answers it twice over. To swear by God's name, acknowledging him as the just judge of one's motives and actions, is itself a command; and an oath of this kind, on such an occasion, can never be called irreligious or profane. Our ideas of delicacy may revolt from the gesture, but once the covenant of which circumcision was the sign is taken into account, the form could not be used without producing reverence and godly fear. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, generalises the principle behind it: swearing is no ordinance peculiar to the church but common to mankind, and is therefore to be performed by whatever signs the usages of a country have appointed for binding the person sworn — which is why honour is done here both to the eternal God, by whom alone such appeals may be made, and, some think, to the covenant of circumcision by the gesture used.
10:
Ten camels go, loaded, and Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, explains the scale: the convoy had to be large enough to keep the servant and the bride safe on the road, and rich enough to represent Abraham's wealth and power adequately at the other end. John Calvin, reformed, puts the same point from the girl's side. Exile is sad enough without poverty for its companion, and no open-hearted young woman would let herself be drawn to a distant country unless she could see she would be provided for; so the presents were the argument. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, adds the custom that made them necessary — in those times a dowry was given for a wife, not received with her — and notes that Abraham left the whole management to his servant's discretion.

That discretion is what "all the goods of his master were in his hand" is taken to authorise. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, and some Jewish interpreters read it of a schedule or inventory carried to show the family he was to treat with. Calvin rejects that reading and takes the clause as the narrative's own explanation of how a servant came to travel with so splendid an equipage: he did it on his own authority, because his master's whole substance was at his disposal. Ellicott renders the phrase "with every good thing of his master's in his hand," which comes to the same practical thing.

Ellicott also asks the question a reader will ask — why did Isaac not go himself? — and answers that his inactivity implies no reluctance: he was the heir, and by Eastern manners the choice was fitly left to a trusted deputy. What is unusual is only the distance and the restriction to one family, and both of those arose from religious considerations. Henry, meanwhile, makes the unnamed servant the moral centre of the chapter, an example to all servants who by serving God and their masters faithfully adorn the doctrine of Christ; and he notes the older reading of the errand, Isaac being a type of Christ, in which fetching a bride from among his own kindred pictures the espousing of the church by the ministry.

At Nahor's city — Haran, as Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch identify it — the camels are made to kneel by the well at evening, when the women come out to draw. The reformed John Gill notes that kneeling is not natural to the animal but taught from birth, and Ellicott observes that the servant did not unlade them until he knew his prayer was heard. He explains the timing too: the well belonged to the whole city and could be used only at a fixed hour, so the man had to wait for the women. Clarke reports the same practice still keeping in Bengal, where companies of women go daily to the pools and rivers for water.
12:
Standing by the well, the servant prays, and it is the passage the commentators weigh most carefully. He asks for good speed this day. The reformed John Gill notices whose God he invokes: not his own, though he plainly was a good man, but the God of his master Abraham — because God had renewed his covenant with Abraham and admitted him to such nearness, and because it was on his master's business and not his own that he stood there. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, makes the same the ground of the plea: as the children of good parents, so the servants of good masters have peculiar encouragement in the prayers they offer for success. Henry also defends praying for so particular a thing at all — we have leave to be particular in commending our affairs to the conduct of divine providence, and those who would have good speed must pray for it. Then the servant proposes a sign: the damsel who answers his request for a drink by offering to water the camels as well. Henry defends it as a prayer rather than a limit set on God — the man did not intend to proceed no further if it were refused — and admires what it asks for: a wife humble and industrious, bred to labour and willing to put her hand to any work, and courteous to a stranger. He notes where the man went to look for her — not to any place of amusement but to the well, expecting to find her rightly employed. Calvin feels the difficulty more sharply. Prescribing to God is unsuitable in prayer, and certainty belongs to God's word rather than to our stipulations; yet the answer given proves the request acceptable, and Calvin concludes that the servant, though he had no promise for this particular, was moved by the secret impulse of the Spirit rather than by the lust of the flesh. Clarke quotes Dodd's defence — that asking a natural sign, one betokening humanity and condescension, keeps the prayer on a rational footing — and then presses past it: this was a case no use of the rational faculties could have decided. His own rule holds both ends. To expect a good end without using the means is enthusiasm; to think any good can be had without God's blessing because the means were used is no better. Plan, scheme and labour like Eliezer, and then commit the whole by faith and prayer to God.

Henry adds one further thing the prayer was asking, beyond a good wife: that God would make the way plain by the concurrence of small circumstances. That God's providence reaches to the smallest occurrences, and serves its own purposes admirably by them, is a good man's comfort as well as his belief; our times are in God's hand, and not only the events but the timing of them. It is wisdom to follow providence and folly to force it — and it is lawful, while setting God's revealed will before us as the rule, to ask that he would direct us by hints of providence in the way of our duty, guiding his people with his eye.
15:
The answer arrives before the request is finished. The reformed John Gill notes that the prayer was offered in the servant's heart, so that the last words were still forming when Rebekah came out; Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, remarks how exactly providence had fitted every circumstance to the need, and in the most punctual manner.

John Calvin, reformed, faces the awkward detail honestly: Rebekah had in fact left her house before the man began to pray, so the speed of the answer is not a matter of her being dispatched at the sound of it. His point is rather that the Lord, at whose disposal both the moments of time and the ways of men lie, had ordered the two movements toward each other. Sometimes God keeps his people in suspense until, wearied with praying, they seem to have lost their labour; here, so that the blessing should not look doubtful, he interposed at once — as the angel came to Daniel before his prayer was ended. Calvin will not let the speed be turned into a rule. Delay is often expedient for us, and it is our own sloth that occasions it; what God has proved by unquestionable examples is not that answers are quick but that the prayers of his people are never in vain, since before they cry he is mindful of their want.

Rebekah herself is then described, and the witnesses read the description as the sign beginning to be fulfilled before a word is exchanged. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, lists what the servant had asked for and finds it all present — handsome and healthful, humble and industrious, courteous and obliging to a stranger. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, watches her conduct at the well and makes it the whole argument: she went down, filled her pitcher, and came up to go home with it. She did not stand and gaze at the strange man and his camels but minded her business, and would not have been diverted from it except by an opportunity of doing good; nor did she enter into conversation with him curiously or confidently, but answered modestly and with all the decorum that became her. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, supplies the physical detail behind "she went down to the well": the water was reached by a flight of steps, which is the usual arrangement where a well is fed by a natural spring, cisterns filled from rain being narrower at the top instead. He quotes a traveller's account of visiting the same well outside Haran, where the steps Rebekah went down are now blocked and the women fill water-skins at the well's mouth; where the troughs still stand at their various heights for camels, for sheep and goats, for kids and lambs; and where the women still wear nose-rings and bracelets of gold, of silver, of brass, and even of glass.

Gill notices one small piece of tact in what follows. The servant did not stop her on the way to the well but waited until she had been down and filled her pitcher, and only then ran to meet her — since the token he had asked for could not be given until she was coming back. Henry draws from the whole scene the reflection that most concerns a reader: those instances of goodness which were once in honour are now in contempt, and Rebekah's daughters are few.
18:
"Drink, my lord," she says, and the reformed John Gill hears deference in the address — seeing the retinue of men and camels she took him for a person of consequence, and made him welcome to as much as he would. Then she goes beyond what was asked. When he had done drinking she said she would draw for the camels also, hasted and emptied her pitcher into the trough, and ran again to the well.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, makes the excess the point of the whole episode. Had Rebekah done no more than Eliezer had prayed for, we might have supposed she was not acting as a free agent but was being moved by the controlling power of God; because she does more than was requested, we see that the kindness sprang from her own benevolence, and her conduct stands in the most amiable light. The sign is fulfilled without being imposed.

Gill dwells on the labour involved — the trough was a hollow of wood or stone set there for the purpose, and she poured into it what remained in her pitcher after the man had drunk, then went back for more, ten camels being a great deal of water. What the servant did while she worked is the one thing in the chapter that draws a rebuke. Clarke cannot get past it: lost in wonder at her simplicity, innocence and benevolence, the man let this delicate young woman draw water for ten camels without once offering to help. He confesses he does not know which to admire more, her condescension or the servant's cold and apparently stupid indifference, and concludes that both are of an uncommon cast.

The others read the man's silence differently, because they read the verb differently. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, notes that the word rendered "wondering" is rare, and that the Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate — followed by Gesenius and Fürst — take it as gazing attentively while holding his peace, in order to know. On that reading the verse is not describing astonishment at all but a man observing everything she said and did and coming carefully to a conclusion about her. Gill's list of what he wondered at runs the other way and is worth having in full: her courtesy to a stranger, her humility in taking such a service upon herself, her readiness and diligence and the quick dispatch she made, the exactness with which her conduct matched the token he had asked for, the providence that had brought him to that place so seasonably, and the timing that brought her to it just then.

John Calvin, reformed, takes the wondering as evidence of real doubt, and does not think it needs excusing away. Faith is never so perfect in the saints as to prevent many doubts; there is no absurdity in a man committing himself generally to God's providence and still wavering amid conflicting thoughts. Faith calms the mind so that we wait patiently, but it does not exempt us from care, since patience itself has to be exercised by anxious expectation until God performs what he promised. Calvin grants that this hesitation flowed from infirmity, and then excuses it on the ground that matters most: the servant did not turn his eyes elsewhere, but sought from the event only a confirmation that God was present with him.
22:
The camels finish drinking and the servant produces gold: a ring of half a shekel's weight and two bracelets of ten shekels for her hands. Where the ring was worn is settled by the witnesses against the English version. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, points out that the man afterwards puts it on her nose, and that the same word is rendered "jewel" elsewhere and placed on the nose in Ezekiel and in a swine's snout in Proverbs; it hung not from the central cartilage but from the pierced left nostril, and such rings are still the usual betrothal present in Arabia, made of gold and silver but also of coral, mother-of-pearl and cheaper stuff; at about a quarter of an ounce it would be no more disfiguring than many ornaments worn now. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, reaches the same conclusion by another road: the singular number rules out a pair of ear-rings, and Symmachus renders the word by a term meaning an ornament for the nose. He takes the bracelets, from a root meaning to clasp, as armlets rather than anklets, since the text says they were for her hands. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, add that he placed the ornaments on her himself, not as a bridal gift but in return for her kindness.

John Calvin, reformed, reads the gift as an act of confidence: a careful servant does not scatter his master's treasure without discretion, so either he knows it is well bestowed or, relying on God's goodness, gives it in faith as an earnest of the marriage to come. Then he turns on his own readers. Does God approve ornaments of this kind, which serve pomp rather than neatness? His answer is a rule of interpretation before a rule of dress: what Scripture relates is not always to be imitated, and while a general command binds inflexibly, to lean on a particular example is dangerous and even absurd. He will not forbid every ornament, but holds that whatever exceeds frugal use is tarnished with vanity, and that here women's desire is insatiable, so that not moderation only but abstinence should be cultivated. Rebekah's jewels he takes to be such as the rich then wore, used sparingly in an upright age — and he still declines to call them faultless. His sharpest word is for those who quote her: they seek in Rebekah a pretext, and do not in like manner conform to the austere life and rustic labour she applied herself to.

Calvin also meets the objection that it ill became a modest maiden to accept jewellery from a stranger. Moses may have passed over the conversation that led up to it; he may relate first what came last, since the question about her family follows immediately; and the simplicity of that age must be allowed for, a girl being able to go alone out of the city because morals then did not require so severe a guard on modesty. The gift, he insists, was not dishonourable but offered toward her parents to facilitate the contract. On the weights he differs from the rest, reading the ring at five shekels rather than half a one, so that it bears some proportion to the bracelets.

Only then does the man ask whose daughter she is, and whether there is room in her father's house to lodge in. The reformed John Gill notes the apparent disorder, since the later retelling puts the question before the gift, and reports Schmidt's reconciliation: he took the ring and bracelets out first, asked, and only then placed them on her. Keil and Delitzsch make the sequence decisive: it was not until Rebekah named Bethuel the son of Milcah and Nahor, and answered the second question cheerfully, with straw and provender enough and room to lodge, that the servant knew this was the wife Jehovah had appointed for Isaac.
26:
The man's response to the answer is not speech to Rebekah but worship. He bowed his head and blessed the LORD God of his master Abraham, who had not left his master destitute of his mercy and his truth: I being in the way, the LORD led me to the house of my master's brethren.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, takes the thanksgiving clause by clause. The man had prayed for good speed and now that he had sped well he gives thanks — what we win by prayer we must wear with praise, since mercies granted in answer to prayer lay us under a particular obligation. He gives thanks while the issue is still only a comfortable prospect and by no means certain, which Henry makes a rule of its own: when God's favours are coming toward us we must meet them with our praises. He gives thanks for another man's mercy, being at that moment negotiating for his master, and we should be as thankful for our friends' mercies as for our own. He gives thanks specifically for being led — he had been in the way and at a loss which course to steer, and Henry finds it very comfortable in doubtful cases to see God leading us, as Israel was led by the pillar of cloud and fire.

Two clauses draw more. The first is the house he was led to. Henry thinks the man counted himself happy, and owned God in it, that he was brought to those of Abraham's kindred who had come out of Ur — for though they had not come on into Canaan but stayed at Haran, they were not idolaters but worshippers of the true God, and inclined to the religion of Abraham's family. God is to be acknowledged, he says, in the providing of suitable partners, and especially of such as agree in religion. The second is "his mercy and his truth." God had promised to build up Abraham's house, and the house had looked destitute of the benefit of that promise; now providence is visibly working toward it. Henry's inference is double: God's faithful ones may be destitute of many worldly comforts but never of God's mercy and truth, since his mercy is an inexhaustible fountain and his truth an inviolable foundation — and it adds much to the comfort of any blessing to see in it the continuance of both.

The reformed John Gill notes what the man had done immediately before, paying his respects to Rebekah for her civility, and Henry observes the incongruity without embarrassment: ear-rings and bracelets sat oddly with a pitcher of water, yet the ornaments she sometimes wore never made her think herself above the labours of a virtuous woman who works willingly with her hands, nor above the services of a child, who while under age differs nothing from a servant. Henry also marks the turn the verse makes — the man turns his wondering into worshipping — and Gill, reading the words as spoken aloud in Rebekah's hearing, points out what they told her: from them she could perceive who he was and where he came from, which is why she runs.
28:
Rebekah runs home, and the household she runs to is described in a way that has told commentators a good deal about it. She tells "them of her mother's house," and Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, insists the words supplied in italics are worse than useless: a sheikh's wife has a tent of her own, and polygamy makes each such family hold closely together. Naturally, too, a girl would show presents of that particular meaning to her mother and the women first. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, allows the same domestic arrangement — in those countries the women's apartments are entirely separate, and grown daughters live there with their mother — while thinking it very likely that Bethuel was in fact dead, since the whole business is conducted by Rebekah's brother. John Calvin, reformed, is content with the simpler reading: she went straight to her mother's chamber because she could tell the matter more easily there, and Bethuel, once informed, joined in sending Laban out. Ellicott notices the same pattern running through the rest of the chapter — Laban acts as Rebekah's representative throughout, and Bethuel is allowed a voice only when the final decision must be given.

Laban's own motive is not left to inference. The reformed John Gill reads the sequence exactly as it stands: it was when he saw the ring and the bracelets on his sister's hands that he ran, concluding the stranger was a rich and generous man from whom a gift might be had, or at least by whom entertainment would not go unrewarded — and Laban's covetousness, Gill notes, is plain from the whole story of him. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, puts it more bluntly still and appeals to the same evidence: here is a man there is something to be got by, so he will be sure to be welcome. Henry cites the proverb that a man's gift makes room for him and prospers whichever way it turns. Ellicott is readier to allow the ordinary motive as well, since such hospitality was in the East almost a matter of course, though he grants Laban's earnestness may have been increased by the sight of the gold.

The greeting is warmer than the motive. "Come in, thou blessed of the LORD; wherefore standest thou without? for I have prepared the house, and room for the camels." Clarke takes this for a usual form of wishing prosperity, since a man blessed of the Lord is worthy of all respect. Gill and John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, both suggest a better ground for it than the jewellery: Rebekah had reported the man's worship and thanksgiving, from which they concluded he was a good man and therefore blessed of God. Henry approves the principle whatever prompted it — those whom God owns we should own too. What strikes Ellicott is the name Laban uses. That he should address a stranger as blessed of Jehovah is remarkable, since the monotheism of Nahor's family was by no means pure; they were not idolaters, but the other gods they served were probably teraphim, as Laban's certainly were later. Most uneducated minds, he observes, even where the religion is in the main true, tend to add superstitions to it, especially by fashioning some lower mediator for themselves.

The welcome is then made good in detail: the camels ungirded, straw and provender given them, water brought for the man's feet and for the feet of the men with him. Clarke notes the order of priority — the beasts first, a good man being merciful to his beast — and that no distinction was made between master and servants when the water came, the journey having fallen as heavily on one as on the other. Henry observes that both house and stable were well furnished and the guest given free use of both.
33:
Food is set before him and he will not touch it. "I will not eat, until I have told mine errand." Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, makes this the measure of the man: though he had come off a journey and come to a good house, business first — the doing of our work and the fulfilling of our trusts, for God or for men, should be preferred before our necessary food. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, notes that the gesture is not eccentric in the East, where a Brahmin may sit down in a house and refuse what is offered until his errand is granted; and he hears an echo of it in the Lord's own words, that his meat was to do the will of him that sent him and to finish his work (John 4:34).

What follows is the longest speech in the book of Genesis, and Henry treats it as a piece of advocacy to be examined for its skill and its honesty together. The opening is a disclosure of identity: I am Abraham's servant. He was welcome before, Henry says, but doubly welcome after that, Abraham's name being known and respected among them. Then a statement of the estate — the LORD hath blessed my master greatly, and he is become great, with flocks and herds, silver and gold, menservants and maidservants, camels and asses — and, immediately after, the fact that makes the estate relevant: Sarah bore a son to his master when she was old, and unto him he hath given all that he hath. The reformed John Gill and Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, both take the inventory as spoken for the family's benefit rather than as boasting; Henry names the two things it was meant to suggest, that Abraham had a very good estate and that he had settled the whole of it on the son for whom the servant is now a suitor.

Then the charge itself, repeated in its own words: thou shalt not take a wife for my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, but shalt go unto my father's house and to my kindred. Henry reads two pieces of tact in the way it is put. It insinuates something pleasing — that Abraham, though removed to a country so far off, still remembered the relations he had left and kept a regard for them, the highest degrees of divine affection not divesting a man of natural affection. And it forestalls an obvious objection. If Isaac were so desirable, why send this distance for a wife rather than marry nearer home? Because, the servant answers, his master's son must not match with a Canaanite. The reason is not a slight on the family being addressed but the whole ground of the errand that has come to them.

Henry adds what the speech is careful to include about Abraham's own confidence. The LORD, before whom I walk, will send his angel with thee and prosper thy way — words in which Henry hears the covenant made earlier, I am God all-sufficient, walk before me. Abraham took encouragement from the testimony of his conscience that he walked before God in a regular course of holy living, and inferred from it that God would prosper the errand. The lesson Henry draws is a rule for reading promises: while we make conscience of our part of the covenant we may take the comfort of God's part of it, and we should learn to apply general promises to particular cases as there is occasion.
39:
The servant now retells his own scruple and Abraham's answer to it, and the retelling is exact: peradventure the woman will not follow me; the LORD, before whom I walk, will send his angel with thee and prosper thy way; then shalt thou be clear from this my oath, when thou comest to my kindred, and if they give not thee one, thou shalt be clear. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, sees the care behind repeating that exchange to the very people it concerns. It shows the servant, in general, to be a cautious man; and particularly, that he had taken pains to preserve their liberty of giving or refusing consent, so that no perjury could be incurred on his side and no compulsion applied on theirs. Their consent might be free or it might be nothing at all.

He then repeats the prayer at the well, and Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, notes how it opens — O LORD God of my master Abraham. Abraham was the friend of God, and the servant uses that standing to give weight and consequence to his own petitions. The reformed John Gill, in passing, disposes of a Jewish embellishment on the journey: the man had come this far by several days' travel, not, as some writers say, in a single day by a miracle.

One word in the retold prayer is not the word used when the meeting was narrated, and both the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott and Clarke stop on it. Where the earlier account called Rebekah a damsel, and then said plainly that she was a virgin, here the servant says almah — a young woman just ripening for marriage. Ellicott traces the same word to Miriam watching her brother's ark, where it is rendered maid, and to the mother of Immanuel at Isaiah 7:14. Clarke presses the sense harder, deriving it from a root meaning to hide or cover, and insisting it means a pure virgin in the proper sense — a woman not uncovered, and in that respect still concealed from man — which he takes to answer to the other term used earlier and to bear on the disputed prophecy.

The sign itself is repeated without alteration: let the damsel who answers drink, and I will draw for thy camels also be the woman the LORD hath appointed. Gill lets the repetition stand as the servant gave it, referring each clause back to what had already been said at the well. Henry's comment on the whole of this stretch of the speech is a rule for hearers rather than for speakers: it is good dealing with those who by prayer take God along with them in their dealings, and the servant is at pains to show that this is what he did before he ever saw their sister.
45:
The one detail the servant is careful to add is that nobody heard him. Before I had done speaking in mine heart, behold, Rebekah came forth. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, thinks he mentions it precisely to forestall a suspicion — that Rebekah might have overheard the prayer and obligingly acted it out. No, says the servant in effect: I spoke it in my heart, so that none heard but God, to whom thoughts are words, and from him the answer came. Adam Clarke reaches the same conclusion from the other side, noting that both accounts of the prayer describe it as mental, and that public prayer would have been out of place there, since the servants with him had no particular interest in petitions whose responsibility was not theirs. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, corrects the idiom slightly and improves it: the Hebrew is more exact than the English — before I had done speaking to my heart.

The rest of the retelling runs as the event ran. She let down her pitcher, gave him drink, watered the camels; he asked whose daughter she was and she named Bethuel the son of Nahor and Milcah; he put the ring upon her nose and the bracelets upon her hands. Ellicott takes the chance to settle the ornament for good: the Hebrew says upon her nose, and it is that mistranslation as "face" which produced the odd marginal guess of a jewel for the forehead in the earlier verse. Then the servant repeats what he did next — bowed his head and worshipped the LORD God of his master Abraham, who had led him in the right way to take his master's brother's daughter for his son. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, lingers on that phrase: God's way is always the right way, and those are well led whom he leads.

The speech ends by putting the matter squarely to them and refusing to press. Now, if ye will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me; and if not, tell me, that I may turn to the right hand or to the left. The reformed John Gill takes the address as made to the whole family and especially to Laban and Bethuel: if the kindness is to be granted, let it be granted sincerely and at once. Henry hears in it the fairness of a man who has dealt fairly — if you will be sincerely kind you will accept, and I have what I came for; if not, do not hold me in suspense — and remarks that those who deal fairly have reason to expect fair dealing. On the closing phrase Clarke will not have more read into it than it says. To turn to the right hand or to the left means simply that he would go elsewhere and seek a proper match for his master's son; the suggestion that he was hinting at the descendants of Ishmael or of Lot he calls fanciful.
50:
The answer is given without haggling and on one ground only: the thing proceedeth from the LORD; we cannot speak unto thee bad or good. John Calvin, reformed, finds that admission the most striking thing in the chapter. Convinced by the man's account that God was the author of this marriage, they judge it unlawful to offer anything by way of contradiction — and these are people whose religion was in part sound and in part infected with vicious errors. If men who had almost fallen away from true religion still held it firmly that God must be obeyed, Calvin asks, how much prompter should our obedience be? As soon as God's will is known, not only should our tongues be silent but all our senses still, since it is an audacious profanation to admit a thought opposed to it. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, notes what they did not object — the distance, Abraham's having forsaken them, his holding no land in possession but only movable wealth — and identifies the two things they trusted: much to the servant's integrity, and more to God's providence, so that their silence gave consent. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, draws the plain conclusion: a marriage is likely to be comfortable when it appears to proceed from the Lord.

Who is speaking has occupied the commentators as much as what is said. The verb "answered" stands in the singular though two names follow, and the reformed John Gill infers that Laban gave the answer with his father's consent — Bethuel being perhaps an old man who had left the management of his affairs to a son who, on Aben Ezra's account, excelled him in wisdom and honour, though Jarchi paints him rather as an impudent man who took upon himself to speak before his father. Gill also reports the alternative that this Bethuel is not the father at all but a younger brother of that name, the father being already dead. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, takes the two for brothers on that reading, with Laban the elder and chief. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, keeps the father alive and explains the order differently: polygamy estranged a father from his own children while each separate family held closely together, which is why Dinah was avenged by her own mother's sons and Tamar by Absalom. Bethuel's consent was finally necessary, but once given, everything active was left to the mother and Laban, and he is not mentioned again.

The consent granted, the servant worships before he does anything else. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, set the order out: thanks to Jehovah with the deepest reverence first, then the presents to the bride and her relations, and only when everything was finished the food he had refused. Calvin says Moses repeats this thanksgiving deliberately and often, because God requires nothing greater from us and the neglect of it betrays the most shameful indolence; the acknowledgment of God's kindness is a sacrifice of sweet savour, more acceptable than all sacrifices. Henry adds the caution that keeps the thanks properly directed: God had sent his angel before the man and so given him success, but when the success came he worshipped God and not the angel.
53:
The presents brought out now are of a different order from the ring and bracelets at the well: jewels of silver, jewels of gold and raiment for Rebekah, and precious things for her brother and her mother. The reformed John Gill describes them as ornaments for women carried along for the purpose, and as proof both of Abraham's wealth and of his liberality in furnishing his servant with such a profusion to bestow. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, counts three motives at once — a real proof of his master's riches and generosity, gratitude for the family's civility, and a further means of ingratiating himself with them. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, note the division: the jewels and raiment to the bride, the precious things to the brother and the mother.

Adam Clarke separates the two occasions by their purpose. The word rendered "jewels," he observes, properly means vessels or instruments, so the gifts may have been of various kinds; what was given at the well was a token of respect, while this appears to be dowry. The word behind "precious things" he traces through its other uses — exquisite fruits and delicacies, precious plants and flowers — and concludes it may mean gifts in general here, though of a rather lower order than what Rebekah received. Ellicott makes the transaction explicit — in ancient times a wife had to be bought, and these were not ornaments merely but articles of substantial use and value; the purchase quickly took a more honourable form in a country of such ceremonial politeness, but the relatives would see to it that the freewill offerings did not fall below the usual standard. That they went to the brother and the mother, and not to the father, has produced a Jewish tradition that Bethuel lay ill at the time and died on the very day of the servant's arrival; Ellicott declines it, since Isaac later speaks of Bethuel in a way that will not suit a dead or negligible man, and suggests instead that polygamy had made the mother's tent the customary destination for such purchase presents, as it had already been the place Rebekah ran to with her news.
54:
Only now does the servant eat, and Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, marks the sequence: he had refused food until he had told his errand, and sat down to it as soon as the answer was favourable. Then, in the morning, he asks to be sent away. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, is struck that he presses it twice, though he and his company were welcome and cheerful where they were. He knew his master would be watching for him and had business at home that wanted him, and so preferred his work to his pleasure. Lingering and loitering, Henry says, no way become a wise and good man; when business abroad is despatched we must not delay our return. John Calvin, reformed, sees more than diligence in the haste. The man is so ardent that he allows no truce to others and no relaxation to himself, and though he behaved as an honest and prudent servant should, Calvin does not doubt that the Lord was impelling him for Isaac's sake — as God watches over his people while they sleep, and moves the dispositions of others to help them.

The family ask for delay: let the damsel abide with us a few days, at the least ten. What that phrase means is genuinely uncertain, and the commentators divide. The Hebrew, Clarke says, is abrupt and obscure — days, or ten — and could be read as a year or ten months, or as a week or ten days. He argues for the shorter sense on the ground that having consented to the match it would be improper to detain her a year, and he backs it with the Septuagint's "about ten days," while noting that Houbigant would emend the text to read "a month of days," with the Syriac behind him. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, records the same Jewish rendering of "a year or ten months" and prefers to take the decade as the name for a third of a month — which would leave the family of Terah measuring time in ten-day periods, as the Egyptians did at one stage of their history. Calvin calls the year-or-months reading forced, and hears in the request only the tender wish of a mother who cannot bear to have her daughter torn from her so suddenly. Henry reads it as evidence that nothing in this world is unmixed: they were pleased to have matched a daughter so well, and when it came to the point were loth to let her go.
57:
The servant will not be delayed — hinder me not, seeing the LORD hath prospered my way — and so the matter is put to Rebekah. The reformed John Gill supposes she had withdrawn to her own apartment out of modesty while the men discussed the business, and had to be called back, or sent for by a servant. Henry approves the appeal warmly, and states the rule in both directions: as children ought not to marry without their parents' consent, so parents ought not to marry them without their own. She is a party principally concerned, and therefore ought to be principally consulted. Calvin guards the same balance from the other side. Bethuel had already given his daughter, but only so far as he was able; now he declines to play the tyrant by thrusting her out unwilling or compelling her against her will. The authority of parents is sacred, yet a middle course must be kept, so that the parties contract spontaneously and with mutual consent.

"Wilt thou go with this man?" And she said, I will go. Calvin defends the promptness of the answer against two possible slanders — that she despised her father's house, or that she was over-eager for a husband — and reads it instead as acquiescence in what her father had authorised and her mother consented to. Ellicott reads it as consistent with everything else shown of her: with matters so plainly providential she would have felt it wrong to make difficulties, and she is ready to go at once, though she will never see her relatives again. Clarke takes her words as the decision of the whole business, and raises one alternative before letting it go: possibly the question meant not whether she would go at all but whether she would go immediately or stay the time her family had asked for. Either way her answer settled it — it plainly appeared to be God's will, and she consented. Henry adds a guess about her motive that fits what she had seen: the servant's piety and devotion had given her an idea of the religion prevailing in the family she was going to, and made her willing to forget her own people and her father's house, where religion had not so much the ascendant.
59:
She is sent away honourably. The reformed John Gill is careful that this was no sulky dismissal in a fit of temper but a willing and affectionate leave-taking, and notes that those who call her their sister here are probably the whole household of her relations. With her go her nurse and her damsels, and the attendants tell their own story. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, names the nurse from a later chapter — Deborah — and thinks it good sense and prudence that a woman who had been a second mother should go with her. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, measures how dear Deborah was, first to Rebekah and afterwards to Jacob, by the lamentation recorded at her death. John Calvin, reformed, explains the office without romanticising it: households had their own nurses among the handmaids, not because mothers wholly neglected the duty but because the care of a child's upbringing was committed to one particular maid.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, and John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, both look back from the damsels to the well. If Rebekah had maids of her own at command, then her going out for water was not necessity but choice — she took pleasure in works of humble industry. Henry also observes what the narrative never mentions: there is nothing said of a portion. Her personal merits were a portion in her; she needed none with her, and none was ever brought into the treaty.

Then the blessing. Thou art our sister; be thou the mother of thousands of millions, and let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them. Ellicott divides it into its two halves — fruitfulness, founded on the primeval command at Genesis 1:28, and victory in war — and notes that the Hebrew says thousands of ten thousands, a million being a number these speakers had no means of expressing. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, take "become thousands of myriads" as hyperbole for an innumerable posterity, and observe that the second half is almost word for word the promise made to Abraham after the binding of Isaac. Henry thinks that is no accident: Abraham's servant had probably told them of the promise lately made to his master, that God would multiply his seed as the stars of heaven and that they should possess the gate of their enemies, and the family's blessing has that promise in view — be thou the mother of that seed. Clarke sets the words among the customs of parting, noting that similar addresses to a daughter leaving her father's house are common still. Henry draws the practical lesson: when our relations are entering a new condition we ought by prayer to commend them to the blessing and grace of God.

Calvin adds only that blessing a bride was a solemn custom in all ages and among all peoples, and that what the word means here is that they prayed her condition might be a happy one. Then Rebekah and her damsels rise, mount the camels, and follow the man.
62:
The meeting happens at evening, in a field, and every witness treats where Isaac was and what he was doing as the point of the scene. He had come from the way of the well Lahai-roi and was dwelling in the south country. The reformed John Gill identifies the well as the one where the angel met Hagar in her flight. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, places it in the Negeb and adds that the oasis round it became Isaac's favourite residence, near Beersheba where Abraham was living; he also notes what the geography implies about the journey — it would have taken some months, during which Abraham's herds would have shifted from station to station, so that Rebekah, arriving at the station furthest from Haran, would have passed all Isaac's other homes on the way. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, conjectures the reverse, that Isaac had come on a visit to his aged father and was waiting there for his bride. John Calvin, reformed, thinks Isaac simply lived apart, the household being too large or the custom being such, and perhaps because Abraham had married again; he is careful to add that this cost Isaac nothing in filial duty — only that they did not live under one roof.

What Isaac was doing in the field turns on a rare Hebrew verb. Ellicott reports that many Jewish commentators translate it "to pray," and derive one of the three Jewish hours of prayer from this act; but the related noun is used of religious meditation in the Psalms, and that sense suits the calm and peaceful Isaac already marked out as the type of the lamb dumb before its slayers. Clarke derives it from a root meaning to bend down, body or mind or both, and pictures a man in deep thought with his eyes on the ground — declining to guess the subject, since a pious man could not be trivially employed. Gill notes that Onkelos and Jonathan render it "to pray," and thinks Isaac's prayers may well have been for the success of his father's servant, in which case they were answered almost as he made them. Calvin leaves the choice open and takes the same view of the outcome: whether he was meditating or praying, the Lord granted him a token of his presence in that joyful meeting.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, and John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, make the scene into a short discourse on solitude. Holy souls love retirement; it does us good to be left alone, and if we have the art of improving solitude we shall find we are never less alone than when alone. The evening is the fit time for such exercises, relieving the fatigue of the day's business and preparing for the night's rest; the open field is the fit place, having the heavens above and the earth around in full view, so that the sight of them leads to the contemplation of their Maker. And Henry's conclusion is the one the narrative supplies: merciful providences are doubly comfortable when they find us well employed and in the way of our duty — as Isaac sets himself, like the prophet on his watch-tower, to see what God will answer, and sees the camels coming.
64:
Rebekah's conduct at the meeting is read the same way by all. She lifted up her eyes, asked the servant who the man walking in the field to meet them was, and hearing it was his master, alighted and covered herself with a veil. Ellicott explains the dismounting as a courtesy still kept in the East, where an inferior meeting a superior descends and comes forward on foot; Rebekah would have been thought bold and disrespectful had she done otherwise. Calvin refuses the reading that she fell from the camel in fright — a woman who had crossed that distance under escort would hardly be terrified by one man — and shows from the sentence itself that the question came first and the dismounting followed from the answer. On the veil the witnesses converge: Clarke calls it a sign of chastity, modesty and subjection; Calvin derives the Latin word for marrying from the custom of giving brides veiled to their husbands, and turns on his own age, whose bridal dress seems contrived for the subversion of all modesty; Ellicott adds the practical detail that the bride's veil was far larger than the everyday one and enveloped the whole body, so that by wrapping herself in it Rebekah was announcing who she was. Henry admires what she did not do — she made no complaint that Isaac had not come to fetch her, nor of the length of the journey nor the hardness of leaving her home — but, having seen providence going before her in the affair, accommodated herself cheerfully to her new relation. He reads both gestures together as the token of a wife's subjection, and applies them: those who by faith are espoused to Christ and would be presented to him as chaste virgins must in conformity to his example humble themselves, as Rebekah alighted when she saw Isaac on foot, and must put themselves in subjection to him who is their head (Ephesians 5:24), as she signified by the veil she put on.

Ellicott sets the moment in the sequence of what the chapter has already shown of her. Besides beauty there has been kindliness of heart, activity, and a courageous submission to the guidance of providence; here we see her modesty and courtesy toward her husband. He adds that the bride's veil was seldom worn after marriage at this early period, which is why both the Egyptians and Abimelech had been free to see Sarah's beauty. Clarke notes that the word for it occurs here for the first time and is of doubtful meaning, most agreeing on a veil or a cloak, and the former as the likelier, since a veil was generally the eastern sign of chastity, modesty and subjection.
66:
The servant tells Isaac all things that he had done, and the reformed John Gill lists what that report must have contained: by what means he found the woman appointed for him, how he came to know her father's house, the welcome he was given there, and the agreement he made with her parents and relations for the wife he has now brought home. It is the fourth time the chapter has gone over the same events, and the account is not summarised even here.

Then the marriage in a single verse. He brought her into his mother Sarah's tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her; and Isaac was comforted after his mother's death. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, takes the last clause first, and does the arithmetic that gives it weight: it was about three years since Sarah died, and Isaac had not until now been comforted concerning it. The wound that affliction gave his tender spirit had bled that long and was never healed until God brought him into this new relation. Henry's comment on the fact is a rule about providence rather than about grief — crosses and comforts are balances to each other, and help to keep the scale even.

What the verse says about Isaac as a son, Henry reads straight across into what it says about him as a husband. She became his wife, and he loved her; and there was every reason in the world why he should, for so ought men to love their wives even as themselves. Those who have approved themselves well in one relation may be hoped to do so in another, and a man who fills up the first station of his life with honour is likely to do the same in those that follow. Henry then states the condition on which the comfort of any such relation actually depends: the duty of it is done, and the comfort of it enjoyed, when mutual love governs — for there the Lord commands the blessing.

The tent is not a detail to pass over either. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, had appealed to this very verse earlier in the chapter as evidence that a wife of standing kept a dwelling of her own, which was why Rebekah ran to her mother's house with her news. Bringing her into Sarah's own tent is therefore what installs her: the household arrangement that framed the beginning of the story is the arrangement that closes it.

Henry's summary of the whole chapter is the one thing the witnesses agree in pressing on a reader. The story is told at extraordinary length, down to minute circumstances that seem hardly worth recording, while matters of great moment and mystery elsewhere in Genesis are despatched in a few words. He does not treat that as an oddity to be explained away. God conceals what is curious from the wise and prudent and reveals to babes what is common and level to their capacity, and rules and saves the world by the foolishness of preaching. The disproportion is deliberate: we are directed to notice God's providence in the little common occurrences of human life, and in them to exercise our own prudence and other graces — because Scripture was not intended for the use of philosophers and statesmen only, but to make all of us wise and virtuous in the conduct of ourselves and our families.
